title: Dual Coding
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Jamie Lee Clark returns dual coding to Allan Paivio's original meaning, the encoding of an idea in long-term memory as both language and image, and argues that the link between the two is what matters for teaching. He contends that the idea has suffered a lethal mutation on its way into classrooms, drifting from a theory of memory into a style of resource design. The piece names five such mutations, from decorative images and read-aloud slides to beautifully designed organisers that students merely receive. Drawing on generative learning research, including a study in which students who generated a representation in the other format outperformed those who stayed in one format, Clark insists that the student must build the connection. He then offers four design rules that protect working memory and five classroom moves, such as explaining an unlabelled diagram aloud or sketching from a closed text, that shift the generative work from teacher to student.
points: Dual coding is a claim about memory, not a slide style; placing a picture beside text makes a connection possible but does not create it.
Decorative images perform worse than no image at all, and reading on-screen text aloud delivers one code twice.
Students who generated a representation in the other format, words from a diagram or a sketch from text, performed best on comprehension.
Four design rules (labels inside the picture, say it or show it, cut images that carry nothing, keep the visual up) protect the conditions but do not produce dual coding.
The most important question is who does the work: the five recommended moves all change what students do rather than improving the resource.
quotes: Dual coding is what happens when an idea is encoded in a student's long-term memory in two forms: as language, and as an image. Each carries something the other doesn't, and a link between them means recalling one can bring back the other.
Somewhere between the research and the classroom, dual coding stopped meaning a theory of how memory stores information and started meaning a way of designing resources.
Dual coding mutates so easily because the resource is the part we can see, so it becomes the part we focus on improving.
The connection has to be built by the student. Give them a picture and ask them to put it into words. Give them words and ask them to represent them visually.
Too often, CPD tells us what to put on the slide, but not what students should do with it.

Those four rules deal with the capacity side of the problem. They prevent three of the five mutations before they take hold. They don’t create dual coding; they protect the conditions in which it can happen.
If you change just one thing this week, take the visual you were about to explain and ask your students to explain it to you instead.
